To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the NMDA and AMPA receptors are differentially involved in the generation and regulation of the locomotor pattern in the lamprey spinal cord.
the NMDA and AMPA receptor mediated synaptic inputs are able to provide a wide range of frequencies of activity to the segmental locomotor networks.

the rate of activity in a network of spinal interneurons that generates locomotor activity is controlled by the relative activation of non-NMDA receptors and NMDA receptors in sensory and suprasynaptic inputs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how sensory and suprasignal inputs to spinal neurons are able to control locomotor rate and pattern.
the mechanisms by which the spinal network can be driven by supraspinal and sensory afferent inputs to produce locomotor activity.
the role of excitatory synaptic transmission via NMDA and/or non NMDA (kainate, AMPA) receptors in the control of the activity of spinal neurons and small neuronal networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the lamprey spinal cord, NMDA receptor activity is not necessary to evoke the locomotor activity, but is necessary to produce an appropriate rate of locomotor activity, whereas non NMDA synapse activity is necessary to evoke the activity, and to produce a continuous rate of activity, which is not dependent on the rate of the input
the NMDA and/or the non NMDA glutamatergic synapses are able to provide a control over the rate of activity of neurons of the lamprey locomotor network.
NMDA receptor-mediated synaptic drive can provide the basis for the generation of rhythmic activity, but it cannot provide the necessary modulation of the activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NMDA and the non-NMDA receptors are not the only two types of receptors involved in synaptic transmission in the CNS.
the NMDA receptors have a major influence on the frequency of the oscillations in the spinal network, whereas the non NMDA components are more important for the generation of the burst pattern.
NMDA receptors are necessary to evoke the oscillations and the rate of oscillation, but that non NMDA synapse are necessary to provide a range of frequencies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NMDA receptors can provide a mechanism for the generation of a wide range of frequencies of oscillatory activity.
we have demonstrated a method to generate a wide range of frequencies of activity by altering the relative contribution of NMDA receptors to the synaptic drive.
NMDA and AMPA receptors have different effects on the rate of oscillations in a network of neurons.
